synthesis.headline: The northern anchor lets go: the week-long cutoff opens into a progressive trough while the southern-tier ridge holds and prepares to migrate east
synthesis.narrative:
The multi-week amplified regime has finally surrendered its northern anchor. The retrograding cutoff that had parked over the northern Plains and Canadian border for days is gone from today's 500 mb map; in its place is an open, slightly negatively tilted longwave trough centered over the north-central US, with heights down near 564 dam and no closed contour to be found. That negative tilt and the absence of a closed low mark this as a progressive, translating and amplifying trough rather than the blocked, near-omega geometry of earlier in the week. The two ridges that flanked it, however, are still standing: a western ridge over the Great Basin (592-594 dam over Utah-Nevada) and a subtropical Atlantic ridge southeast of the Carolinas (also near 592 dam), leaving split flow over the eastern CONUS. The organizing story, then, is a northern tier that has gone progressive while the southern-tier ridging persists and is poised to relocate.

Today's centers of action ring that progressive trough and its trailing cold front. The most active corridor runs from a morning cluster of strong-to-severe storms near the Iowa-Missouri border, where an upstream disturbance rotating through the trough should reignite convection into eastern Iowa this afternoon (SPC Marginal, episodic before evening); WPC pairs this with a Slight Risk for excessive rainfall from the Upper Great Lakes and mid-Mississippi Valley into the central Plains. The North American Monsoon is the second focus, with SPC's higher-confidence downburst threat again in southeastern Arizona — steep lapse rates and a dry sub-cloud layer supporting 60-80 mph microbursts — plus upslope storms off the Raton Mesa into the southern High Plains. The third is the Southeast, where deep tropical moisture streaming up the western flank of the Atlantic ridge supports a Slight Risk for flash flooding on the South Carolina coast. In Canada, a 1034 hPa Pacific high offshore of British Columbia extends a ridge into the western interior and keeps the Cordillera and Prairies quiet, while a 992 hPa low near the Great Lakes/border — the surface reflection of the progressive trough — trails fronts that can push a rain shield into southern Ontario and Quebec, and a quasi-stationary boundary across the Manitoba-Ontario corridor is the interior convective trigger. The North Atlantic lows remain well north of the Maritimes, brushing only Atlantic Canada with their trailing fronts.

Aloft, the pieces fit. The jet wraps the trough base and arcs northeast toward the Great Lakes and New England at 50-70 kt, supplying the forcing for the front; the sharp Air Mass RGB boundary from the central Plains through the Ohio Valley to the mid-Atlantic marks that baroclinic zone and implied jet corridor, with green tropical air banked on its southeast side. Note the distinction the imagery draws: a compact, saturated dry streamer curling cyclonically from Texas into Tennessee and Kentucky is a genuine dry intrusion / elevated-PV feature, whereas the broad orange-red over the southern Plains, southern Rockies and northern Mexico is warm, subsident ridge-top air, not a stratospheric signature. On the regime question, the ensemble pair argues relocation rather than collapse. The 6-10 day (Aug 10-14) shows only a modest western ridge (+40 to +50 m over the Great Basin, zero line back to the Rockies) against a deep Arctic trough over the Archipelago and Hudson Bay (near -150 m) — which would read as a weakening ridge in isolation. But the 8-14 day (Aug 12-18) rebuilds and expands that ridge, pushing the 576 dam contour into Montana and the Dakotas with the core over the central and northern Rockies into the northern Plains — the opposite of a shrinking or Southwest-retreating ridge. WPC's extended discussion bridges the two: the long-anchored Southwest upper high holds hazardous heat through the weekend before it finally begins to break down, with ridging then expanding east over the Central US and Southeast next week. So this is a genuine eastward migration of the amplified ridge — the Southwest core does erode as monsoon moisture increases — riding alongside a persistently progressive northern stream, not a wholesale regime collapse. That continues, and confirms, yesterday's read of a ridge relocating north and east rather than dying.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-summer North America running on script: an entrenched Southwest heat regime under the western ridge, a monsoon in full swing over Arizona and New Mexico (and expected to reach Utah and Colorado next week), and marginal severe and heavy-rain threats strung along the frontal boundaries that ring the ridge. The ENSO backdrop is a steady cold-to-warm transition — the ONI table runs from a weak La Niña in late 2025 (near -0.5) through neutral to a warm peak around +0.98 in April-June 2026, placing early August under a warm-ENSO/weak El Niño influence, though the provided table does not extend past spring. Both hurricane basins remain quiet against the climatological ramp toward the September peak: NHC expects no Atlantic, Caribbean or Gulf development over the next seven days, while the eastern Pacific carries two tropical waves at just 20 percent formation odds and near-zero chances through 48 hours.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no mesoscale discussions active and none in the past six hours, consistent with a marginal, boundary- and terrain-driven severe day. Localized signals worth watching: 60-80 mph microburst potential under monsoon convection in southeastern Arizona, and evaporatively cooled severe gusts off Raton Mesa storms into the southern High Plains; the Iowa-Missouri cluster as it works east; and urban/small-stream flooding along the excessive-rainfall axes on the South Carolina coast, the Upper Great Lakes, and the central Plains. Persistent wildfire smoke continues to degrade air quality across the Pacific Northwest and Great Basin, with alerts in effect for sensitive groups, and WPC carries Moderate HeatRisk (3/5) building over the next couple of days. In Canada, the quasi-stationary front across the Manitoba-to-Ontario corridor is the likely focus for interior convective initiation.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This is the WPC 1200Z surface analysis for 5 August 2026. The dominant features are a broad 1023 mb high centered over the central Atlantic coast and a 1021 mb high over the central Plains, both modest summer values that reflect fair-weather ridging rather than strong anticyclonic forcing. The most dynamically active zone is across the central and southern Rockies into the southern Plains, where a weak low near 1007-1008 mb over the southern Rockies and a sprawling lee trough extending into New Mexico and western Texas are focusing surface moisture convergence, with dewpoints in the upper 60s and low 70s F visible in that corridor, consistent with ongoing or impending convective development. A cold front extends from a low near the Great Lakes southward through the mid-Mississippi Valley and into Texas, with its southern tail showing classic warm-sector dewpoints in the upper 70s F across the Gulf Coast states; the pressure gradient along that frontal zone appears tight enough near the Great Lakes low to support organized lift there. A separate frontal boundary — appearing to be a stationary or warm front — drapes across the Mid-Atlantic and southern New England, where another 1019 mb low sits offshore; the gradient there is slack, though the frontal boundary itself marks the sharpest moisture discontinuity on the eastern seaboard. Across the Pacific Northwest and the northern Rockies, gradients are loose and the pattern is largely unforced at the surface.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC 0000Z 5 August 2026 surface analysis shows a broad high centered near 1034 hPa sitting over what appears to be the northeastern Pacific, roughly offshore of the British Columbia coast, with an elongated ridge extending southeastward toward the western United States and helping suppress organized frontal activity across the Canadian Cordillera and adjacent plains. A cluster of lows in the 976 to 999 hPa range occupies the North Atlantic sector well north of the Maritime provinces, with associated frontal boundaries trailing southwestward; the closest warm and cold frontal segments appear to reach toward Atlantic Canada and the northeastern seaboard, where the gradient tightens and would support enhanced lift. Over the Canadian interior, pressure gradients between the Pacific high to the west and a modest low near 1006 hPa that appears positioned somewhere over the central or southern prairies region are relatively slack, though a quasi-stationary frontal boundary with a qs notation arcs across what looks like the Manitoba-to-Ontario corridor, marking the likely focus for convective initiation in that area. Along the US border from the Great Lakes eastward, a surface low near 992 hPa with attendant frontal structure implies a tightening gradient and a rain shield that could extend north into southern Ontario or Quebec, though the exact position of those fronts relative to the provincial boundaries is difficult to resolve precisely at this chart scale. The Arctic portions of the frame show several lows in the 983 to 1003 hPa range over the Archipelago and surrounding waters, which are unremarkable at that latitude in summer and do not appear to connect directly to the main Canadian provincial weather pattern.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary: At 500 mb valid 1200 UTC 5 August 2026, a deep longwave trough is centered over the north-central United States, with heights falling to near 564 dam over the northern Plains and a pronounced meridional amplitude spanning from roughly the Canadian border southward to the central Plains. The green shading, which marks the region of strongest winds, outlines an implied jet corridor wrapping anticyclonically around the trough base and extending northeast toward the Great Lakes and New England, with wind barbs in that corridor suggesting speeds in the 50-70 knot range. The trough axis appears to carry a slight negative tilt — the base is displaced slightly east of the northern portion — which is consistent with a progressive, amplifying shortwave rather than a blocking pattern; there is no closed height contour visible on the chart, so this remains an open, translating trough rather than a cutoff low. A 500 mb ridge axis is evident across the Intermountain West, anchored by the surface high labeled over the Great Basin near Utah/Nevada, with heights near 592-594 dam there, while a separate subtropical ridge center labeled H sits over the western Atlantic southeast of the Carolinas, with heights also near 592 dam, producing a split-flow geometry over the eastern CONUS. Overall the pattern reads as progressive rather than blocked, with no stacked high-over-low couplet at a common longitude that would satisfy a Rex block definition.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB valid 05 Aug 2026 at 1401Z shows a broad orange-red expanse across the southern Plains into the central Rockies and northern Mexico, consistent with dry, subsident mid- and upper-tropospheric air beneath what is likely a summertime upper-level ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. A sharply defined airmass boundary arcs from the central Plains northeastward through the Ohio Valley toward the mid-Atlantic coast, where the transition from orange-red to green is abrupt enough to mark the implied jet corridor; the green tones on the eastern flank indicate deep tropical moisture streaming northward along that boundary. A more compact, elongated dry streamer with somewhat more saturated orange color wraps cyclonically around what appears to be a weak trough axis positioned near the central Mississippi Valley, curling from Texas northeastward into Tennessee and Kentucky — that tighter, more isolated geometry on the cyclonic side of the flow is more consistent with a genuine dry intrusion or elevated PV feature than the broader ridge-top orange to its west. Scattered clusters of white high cold cloud tops are visible across the Gulf Coast states, the Caribbean, and along the moist eastern flank of the boundary, indicating active deep convection in the tropical moisture pool.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: The polar jet and its associated airmass boundary are clearly depicted across the upper portion of the frame as a sharp transition from the deep red-orange of dry upper-tropospheric air over Canada and the northern US to the blue-purple tones of colder air masses pushing into the high latitudes; a well-organized cyclonic swirl sits over the North Atlantic east of Newfoundland, with a compact, curved cloud shield consistent with a mature extratropical system. Over the eastern Pacific between roughly 10 and 20 degrees North, a cluster of bright white convective tops is visible west of Mexico, and a second area of deep convection appears over the western Caribbean and Central American landmass, both embedded within the broad green tropical moisture pool. Across the tropical Atlantic, the green airmass signal is relatively continuous with only modest convective clusters, and no clearly organized wave-induced convective envelope is apparent at this resolution. A sharp, elongated dry-air intrusion in saturated orange-red is visible on the poleward flank of the South Pacific near the bottom-left of the frame, wrapping cyclonically around what appears to be a Southern Hemisphere extratropical system, which is the appropriate geometry for a high-PV stratospheric intrusion signature in this product. Southern South America and the far southern oceans also show active extratropical systems in blue and white tones consistent with cold, cloud-laden airmasses rotating through the Southern Hemisphere westerlies.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The highest-confidence above-normal signal on this chart sits across the south-central and southeastern United States, where probabilities reach the 90-100% range across Texas, Oklahoma, the Gulf Coast states, and Florida, with the 80-90% contour extending north through the lower Mississippi Valley and Carolinas. A secondary above-normal maximum at 70-80% probability covers a broad swath of the Intermountain West and northern Rockies, while the signal weakens to the 40-50% leaning-above range across the northern Plains and Pacific Northwest. The only region without a clear above-normal tilt is a near-normal area centered on the upper Great Lakes and upper Midwest, with the Aleutian Islands showing a small below-normal signal in the inset. The spatial structure of this outlook, with strong above-normal probabilities anchored in both the Southwest-to-southern Plains corridor and the Southeast simultaneously, is consistent with a broad, persistent upper-level ridge dominating the southern tier of the country through the valid period August 10-14, rather than a pattern in transition. Alaska's interior shows 60-70% above-normal probability as well, suggesting the implied ridging extends into high latitudes, though this chart does not plot the upper-level field directly.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
The chart is the CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and anomaly forecast, valid 10-14 August 2026, made 9 August 2026. Heights are contoured in solid green at 60 m intervals (labeled as four-digit meter values: 5460, 5640, 5700, 5760, 5820, 5880 m, equivalent to roughly 546-588 dam), and anomalies are dashed — red positive, blue negative — also in meter units at 60 m intervals, with labeled values running in the tens of meters as expected.

The dominant feature is a deep negative anomaly center over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and northern Hudson Bay, where anomalies reach approximately -150 m (-15 dam), co-located with a closed low in the height field near 546 dam. A secondary negative center is evident over the northeastern Pacific, offshore of the Alaska panhandle, near -60 m (-6 dam). Positive anomalies are confined to a broad but modest ridge over the interior western United States and the subtropical Pacific, with values near +40 to +50 m (+4 to +5 dam) over the Great Basin and southwestern Canada; these values are not strong by amplification standards.

The ridge axis runs roughly north-south near 110-115°W, from the southwestern US northward into Alberta, but the zero-anomaly line crosses well into the western interior of North America — reaching approximately the Rockies or just east — meaning the positive anomaly footprint does not extend strongly into the Pacific Northwest or British Columbia. The trough axis associated with the Arctic low extends southward through Hudson Bay toward the Great Lakes region, consistent with a positively tilted trough digging into central Canada. Overall the pattern implies a partially amplified but weakening western ridge with the main amplitude concentrated in the Arctic trough; the flow across the northern tier of North America is more meridional than zonal, but the modest western ridge anomaly values suggest any amplification there is not intensifying.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This chart is a 500 mb heights and anomalies prognostic valid August 12–18, 2026, made August 9, 2026 — it is the 8–14 day product as described, with green solid contours for heights (60 dam intervals) and dashed contours for departures from normal (also in dam).

The dominant feature is a deep, closed low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with heights near 546 dam at its core, representing a strong negative anomaly of roughly –9 dam or greater in that region. A prominent ridge extends from the subtropical Pacific northward into the interior western United States and the central Rockies, with the ridge axis running approximately from northern Mexico through the Great Basin toward the northern Plains; the 576 dam and 582 dam contours are displaced well northward across the contiguous U.S., consistent with a positive anomaly of around +3 to +6 dam across much of the western and central lower 48. Critically, the ridge core as drawn appears centered over the central and northern Rockies into the northern Plains rather than having retreated to the Southwest — the 576 dam contour extends into Montana and the Dakotas, supporting a notable warm, high-pressure signal over that region. A secondary positive anomaly near +3 dam is apparent over the southeastern United States and western Atlantic near the 588 dam contour. The trough axis associated with the Arctic low dips southward into central Canada, with the implied flow pattern suggesting a relatively zonal but amplified pattern across the continent.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Slight Risk (level 2) excessive rainfall Wednesday over South Carolina Coast and Upper Great Lakes/Middle Mississippi Valley into Central Plains, with localized flash flooding likely in urban areas and small streams. Marginal Risk (level 1) Thursday over Northeast, Great Lakes, Mississippi Valley, Central/Southern Plains, and Southwest as boundaries trigger continued convection through Friday morning. Monsoonal moisture will produce moderate to heavy rain over Southwest late afternoon through Friday. Third front moving into Upper Midwest/Northern Plains Thursday-Friday with scattered thunderstorms. Persistent smoke from ongoing fires affecting Pacific Northwest and Great Basin with air quality alerts in effect; sensitive populations at risk. Warming temperatures producing Moderate Heat Risk (3/5) over next couple days.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary:
Marginal risk of severe thunderstorms across mid Mississippi Valley, southern High Plains, and southeastern Arizona valid through tomorrow morning.

Mid Mississippi Valley: A cluster of strong to severe storms near the Iowa-Missouri border this morning may persist eastward with uncertain severe potential. Additional development expected later today as an upstream disturbance moves through the upper trough into northeast Iowa and Iowa, with moderate buoyancy and sufficient shear supporting storm organization. Episodic severe risk possible before evening weakening.

Southeastern Arizona: Strong heating of moist morning airmass will trigger orographic convection over higher terrain, spreading to lower deserts early evening. Steep lapse rates support microburst risk with 60-80 mph downdraughts. Insufficient model confidence prevents upgrade despite threat.

Southern High Plains: Scattered diurnal development expected over Raton Mesa vicinity from upslope flow. Evaporative cooling from dry sub-cloud layer may produce localized severe gusts 60-80 mph.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No organized convective threat is currently being monitored by SPC. No mesoscale discussions have been issued in the past 6 hours.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
ATLANTIC: No tropical cyclone formation expected over the next 7 days across the Atlantic, Caribbean, and Gulf of America.

EAST PACIFIC: Two tropical waves are being monitored. A wave in the western east Pacific is producing disorganized activity with marginally conducive conditions for slow development as it moves westward at 10-15 mph; 20 percent formation chance through 7 days. A second wave over the central east Pacific has limited activity but could see more favorable conditions develop over the weekend into early next week; also 20 percent 7-day formation chance. Both systems show near 0 percent development probability through 48 hours.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows weak La Niña conditions currently (SON 2025 at -0.51 anomaly), gradually weakening through early 2026. The phase transitions to neutral conditions by late winter (DJF 2026 at -0.37), then shifts toward weak El Niño by spring. By late spring 2026 (AMJ), anomalies reach +0.98, indicating transition to moderate El Niño. Overall trend is clear warming of equatorial Pacific waters over the forecast period.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA is weakly negative and declining over the past week, averaging -0.70; this offers only modest directional support away from western ridging in midsummer. AO has swung sharply positive, rising from -0.05 to +0.37 over seven days, currently -0.35, suggesting reduced high-latitude blocking tendency. NAO has turned notably negative, dropping from +0.19 to -0.90 and holding near -1.28, which could favor eastern Atlantic blocking or cutoff systems. Summer teleconnection amplitudes are inherently weak; these patterns provide directional cues rather than firm constraints.
